directions.title: Whose belief is a rating? The framing check
directions.odds_event: (a) "how likely is it that this statement is true" and (b) "how confident are you that this statement is true" are interchangeable: Q ≥ 0.90 and |mean shift| < 3 points.
directions.question: When an AI rates how likely a statement is true, is that the same as rating how confident it is?
known: Program 1 mostly asked how likely a statement was true, and only once how confident the model was.
Our data say nothing directly: the two wordings were never compared. Philosophers predict they match.
directions.cheapest_test: Ask about the same claims four ways: how likely it is true, how confident you are, how confident another AI would be, how confident Sam would be; compare.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 40 cents of API to ask the model about the same statements in two ways, "how likely is this true?" and "how confident are you?", to see whether its rating is really its own view? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the two ways give the same answers)?
engine_only: the exact bar: agreement Q ≥ 0.90 and mean shift under 3 points
secondary: the third-person framing also matches
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and program 1's 160 claims, that 'how likely is this true' and 'how confident are you' are interchangeable: they share about 77% of reproducible item variation, below the 90% bar.
directions.prior_work_line: Philosophy (Gordon 1986; Schwitzgebel 2008; no data) predicts pass: confidence in p is read off a judgment of p. LLM work predicts fail: Kim and Kang 2026 (arXiv 2605.27752, five open LLMs) find instruction wording the main driver of stated-confidence shifts; Suzgun et al. 2024 (arXiv 2410.21195; GPT-4, Claude 3, Llama 3) score first-person belief items 54.4% against 80.7% third-person. Settled om-p2-1: fail, Q 0.77 on Haiku.
prior_work_sources: Gordon 1986, Folk psychology as simulation, DOI 10.1111/j.1468-0017.1986.tb00324.x (reads D29, secondary)
Schwitzgebel 2008, The unreliability of naive introspection, DOI 10.1215/00318108-2007-037 (reads D27)
Kim and Kang 2026, Same Answer, Different Confidence: Protocol Sensitivity in LLM Confidence Calibration, arXiv 2605.27752
Suzgun et al. 2024, Belief in the Machine: Investigating Epistemological Blind Spots of Language Models, arXiv 2410.21195
om-p2-1 result, programs/other-minds/results/p2-1-framing.md
directions.prior_work_search: reads D27, D29, B17, B9; novelty.md paper list; arXiv abstracts 2605.27752 and 2410.21195 opened; web search for 'how confident' vs 'how likely' item-level comparison found none

directions.title: Perspective-filter equivalence
directions.short: Is belief just a filtered world?
directions.odds_event: Item-level Q of (i) the full third-person story ("how likely is it that Noor believes X") against (ii) the filtered first-person story with the unseen events deleted ("how likely is X") is ≥ 0.80.
directions.question: Is judging what someone else believes the same as judging what is true using only what they saw?
known: Program 1: the model's judgment depends on the text it reads, which predicts the two will match.
One earlier study tried this and found only a small, partial overlap, on about 40 items.
directions.cheapest_test: Ask how likely a story character believes something; then, in a first-person version showing only what the character saw, ask how likely it is true. Compare item by item.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $1.25 of API to find out whether the model's guess at what a story character believes is nothing more than its own judgment, made from that character's side of the story? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means yes, it is just that)?
engine_only: the exact bar: agreement Q ≥ 0.80 story by story
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and BigToM stories, that attributing Noor's belief is just judging the world from her filtered evidence: the two share about half the item variance, almost none within condition.
directions.prior_work_line: Predicts fail, partial overlap. Aoki and Kawahara 2025 (IJCNLP-AACL SRW; Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-72B): mapping third-person onto filtered first-person representations flips at most 0.23 net on about 40 items. Wilf et al. 2023 (arXiv 2311.10227; Llama-2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4): filtering to what the character knows raises false-belief accuracy 3 to 62 points, so the two readings differ wherever filtering helps. Settled om-p2-2: fail, Q 0.50 on Haiku.
prior_work_sources: Aoki and Kawahara 2025, Testing Simulation Theory in LLMs' Theory of Mind, ACL Anthology 2025.ijcnlp-srw.9 (reads B20, full)
Wilf et al. 2023, Think Twice: Perspective-Taking Improves Large Language Models' Theory-of-Mind Capabilities, arXiv 2311.10227
Sclar et al. 2023, SymbolicToM, arXiv 2306.00924 (reads A7)
om-p2-2 result, programs/other-minds/results/p2-2-perspective.md
directions.prior_work_search: reads A7, B20, A15; arXiv 2311.10227 full text opened for the per-model table

directions.title: SimpleToM decomposed: is the "stated but not used" gap a memory effect?
directions.odds_event: A wrong answer planted as the model's own moves behaviour answers toward it at least 10 points more than the same answer credited to another reader, with the CI excluding 0.
directions.question: When an AI says correctly what a character believes but then mispredicts what they do, is that memory, not understanding?
known: Models state a character's belief, then fail to use it; showing their own earlier answer fixes most of that.
Program 1: consistency is memory, and the model sticks to its own past answers but ignores others'.
directions.cheapest_test: Before story questions, hide the model's earlier answer about the character's belief, or plant a wrong one labelled as its own or as another reader's; see what moves.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $1.75 of API to find out whether models that say a character doesn't know something, then predict the character will act as if they did, are failing at understanding minds or only at remembering their own earlier answer? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it is mostly memory)?
engine_only: the exact bar: a planted wrong answer labelled as the model's own pulls at least 10 points more than one credited to another reader
secondary: the record, not the question, carries the reminder effect
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and 581 lower-severity SimpleToM stories, that the 'stated but not used' gap is memory of the model's own answer: a planted own answer pulled less than another reader's (om-p2-3 itself was untestable: a refusal).
directions.prior_work_line: Predicts pass. Kumaran et al. 2025 (arXiv 2507.03120, Gemma 3 12B): change of mind 13.1% with its own answer shown against 32.5% hidden; the same answer credited to another LLM gives 33.2% against 31.3%, no effect. SimpleToM (Gu et al. 2024, arXiv 2410.13648): showing the model its own mental-state answer lifts GPT-4o behaviour accuracy 49.5 to 82.8. Settled om-p2-3b: fail, reversed; the other-credited answer pulled more (Δ −0.053) on Haiku.
prior_work_sources: Kumaran et al. 2025, How Overconfidence in Initial Choices and Underconfidence Under Criticism Modulate Change of Mind in LLMs, arXiv 2507.03120 (reads B18; HTML re-opened: 33.2 vs 31.3 confirmed, position of the other-LLM answer not stated in main text)
Gu et al. 2024, SimpleToM, arXiv 2410.13648 (reads A10, full)
Riemer et al. 2025, Position: theory of mind benchmarks are broken, arXiv 2412.19726 (reads A11; social prompting does not fix action, the opposite sign)
om-p2-3b result, programs/other-minds/results/p2-3b-simpletom-lowsev.md
directions.prior_work_search: reads A10, A11, B18; arXiv 2507.03120 HTML opened to check the flagged 33.2% figure

directions.title: Interpersonal replication against program 1's ground truth
directions.odds_event: Arm (a) [self-prediction, in a fresh context] is no more accurate than arm (b) [observer: the same transcript, labelled as an AI assistant called Sam] (the CI of the error difference includes 0 or favours (b)), and (a) and (b) correlate r ≥ 0.7 across conditions.
directions.question: Can an AI predict its own quirks any better than it predicts the same quirks in another, similar AI?
known: In people, outside observers predict subjects' own reports of what swayed them almost exactly.
Program 1: the model had no inside edge on its own errors, and we have its measured quirks to score against.
directions.cheapest_test: Show the model program 1's test setups and ask it to predict its own answers, then a similar AI's, then from a one-line summary; score each against what happened.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $1.25 of API to check whether the model predicts its own quirks any better than it predicts the quirks of another assistant just like it? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means no better: it reads itself like a stranger)?
engine_only: the exact bar: self-prediction error no smaller than for "Sam", and the two sets of predictions correlate r ≥ 0.7
directions.prior_work_line: Predicts pass. Nisbett and Wilson 1977 (DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.84.3.231): observers given one-line descriptions matched subjects' reports at .77 to .99 and were no less accurate. Blandfort and Pawar 2026 (arXiv 2609.09899): self-report predicts own behaviour at r +0.04; other models' self-answers predict a target at least as well. Xiao et al. 2025 (arXiv 2509.24988): self-correctness prediction no better than an unrelated LLM. om-p2-4: undetermined (self 0.054, Sam 0.097).
prior_work_sources: Nisbett and Wilson 1977, Telling more than we can know, DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.84.3.231 (reads D1, full)
Blandfort and Pawar 2026, Strangers to Themselves: What Language Models Say About Themselves Is Generic, arXiv 2609.09899 (abstract opened)
Xiao et al. 2025, Generalized Correctness Models, arXiv 2509.24988 (abstract opened)
Song et al. 2025, Privileged Self-Access Matters for Introspection in AI, arXiv 2508.14802 (reads B9)
om-p2-4 result and audit, programs/other-minds/results/p2-4-interpersonal.md, ledger/audits/om-p2-4.md
directions.prior_work_search: reads D1, D2, B7, B9; web search 'LLM self-prediction versus other model 2026' and 'cross-model prediction self-knowledge'; abstracts 2609.09899 and 2509.24988 opened
directions.novelty_line: Binder et al. 2024 (arXiv 2410.13787) report that a finetuned model predicts its own behaviour better than a second model trained on the same facts, while Song, Hu and Mahowald 2025 (arXiv 2503.07513) and Blandfort and Pawar 2026 (NeurIPS 2026 AI4GOOD workshop) find no self-specific advantage by prompting; our prompt-only "you" versus "Sam" contrast on anchoring effects is undetermined, leaning self. That models misreport what moved their answers is in print (Turpin et al. 2023, arXiv 2305.04388; Chen et al. 2025, arXiv 2505.05410), but no paper states that reported anchor influence runs opposite to measured uptake, the same under self and other labels. Search: WebSearch for "LLM self-prediction vs other-model prediction introspection", "self-report anchoring influence LLM", "Nisbett Wilson 1977"; arXiv abstract pages for each lead.

directions.title: Egocentric leakage: Carruthers's model 3 against model 4
directions.odds_event: In arm (b) [the model's own earlier answer is planted; Sam has read the same question but not that answer], the Sam rating moves at least 0.10 points per point of planted displacement, with the CI excluding 0.
directions.question: Does what an AI itself believes seep into what it says someone else believes, even someone who lacks its information?
known: People project what they know onto those who don't; in AIs this is shown only in anecdotes.
Program 1: a planted 'own' earlier answer moves the model's own rating. Whether it moves Sam's is untested.
directions.cheapest_test: Plant a fake earlier answer as the model's own, then ask for its rating and for the rating of Sam, who never saw that answer; check whether Sam's moves too.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $1 of API to check whether the model's own opinion leaks into what it says someone else believes, when that someone could not know what the model knows? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means yes, its own view leaks in)?
engine_only: the exact bar: the other's rating moves at least 0.10 points per point the model's own view is pushed
secondary: a curse-of-knowledge gap of at least 5 points
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and program 1's 16 vignettes, that a planted own answer reaches Sam's rating only through the model's own revised view: Sam's rating followed it more (+0.14).
directions.prior_work_line: Predicts pass. Choi, Hong and Kim 2024 (arXiv 2407.12007; GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama 2 70B, Mixtral): an option inserted as the model's own choice shifts its estimate of peers choosing it by 0 to 40.5 points (Claude 3: 0 to 25.5), below Ross et al. 1977's 17 to 21.5. No self re-rating or third-party arm. om-p2-5: Sam moved 0.50, map's event met, frozen rule failed (Sam exceeded own, +0.14).
prior_work_sources: Choi, Hong and Kim 2024, People will agree what I think: Investigating LLM's False Consensus Effect, arXiv 2407.12007 (full HTML opened, Table 2)
Epley et al. 2004, Perspective taking as egocentric anchoring and adjustment, DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.87.3.327 (reads D12)
Ryskin and Brown-Schmidt 2014, Do adults show a curse of knowledge, PLoS ONE 9(3) e92406 (reads C14; d = 0.20, arm (a) only)
novelty.md item 6
om-p2-5 result and audit, programs/other-minds/results/p2-5-egocentric.md, ledger/audits/om-p2-5.md
directions.prior_work_search: reads D12, C13, C14; novelty.md item 6; arXiv 2407.12007 full text opened for models and per-story numbers
directions.novelty_line: The manipulation is in print: Choi, Hong and Kim (2024, arXiv 2407.12007; NAACL Findings 2025) fed GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama 2 70B and Mixtral one option as the model's own choice and found its estimate of how many peers would choose it shifted, by 20 points on Claude 3 Opus in one story (a false-consensus effect, generally smaller than in Ross et al. 1977's human data). They did not compare the pull on others with the pull on the model's own re-rating, and showed no third party's number for contrast. Ours found the prediction of another mind moved more than the model's own answer (0.50 against 0.36 of the way; a third party's number 0.02), with the excess coming from upward plants only, so it may be a scale artefact. Search: paper/novelty.md, 2026-11-05 (arXiv searches on false consensus in LLMs, egocentric projection, self-other anchoring), by a claude-fable-5-1 session on the novelty-check branch (93f47af); carried here by the informed-engine session.

directions.title: Is "own" a position or a label?
directions.short: Own: a position or a label?
directions.odds_event: The label effect (own minus Sam, pooled over position) is at least 0.15 uptake, with the CI excluding 0, and larger than the position effect.
directions.question: Does an AI stick to an earlier answer because it is labelled 'yours', or just because it sits where the AI speaks?
known: Program 1: the model sticks to its own earlier answer and ignores another's, but wording and place differed.
Elsewhere, flipping who is said to have written a text changes how much a model favours it.
directions.cheapest_test: Put the same earlier number in the AI's turn or the user's, labelled 'your answer' or 'Sam's answer', with identical wording, and measure how much it pulls.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 80 cents of API to find out whether the model sticks to its earlier answers because they are labelled "yours", or only because of where they sit in the conversation? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the label matters more)?
engine_only: the exact bar: the label effect is at least 0.15 and larger than the position effect
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and program 1's 16 items at +/-30, that the 'yours' label carries the own-answer pull: the label added +0.08, the assistant-turn position +0.23.
directions.prior_work_line: Mixed. Khullar et al. 2026 (arXiv 2603.04582; Claude 3.5 Haiku, Sonnet 4, Opus 4.1 among ten): explicit authorship labels move scores under 0.5 of 10, while the artefact's transcript position cuts monitor AUROC 0.99 to 0.92, predicting fail. Panickssery et al. 2024 (arXiv 2404.13076): reversing the source label moves GPT-4 self-preference 0.73 to 0.32, predicting pass. Settled om-p2-6: fail, position +0.23, label +0.08 (Haiku); neither on Sonnet or Opus.
prior_work_sources: Khullar, Hopkins, Wang and Roger 2026, Self-Attribution Bias: When AI Monitors Go Easy on Themselves, arXiv 2603.04582 (full HTML opened)
Panickssery, Bowman and Feng 2024, LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations, arXiv 2404.13076 (reads B13, full)
Tsui 2025, Self-Correction Bench, arXiv 2507.02778 (full HTML opened)
Kumaran et al. 2025, arXiv 2507.03120 (reads B18; other-LLM label removes the effect, position of that answer unstated)
novelty.md item 3
om-p2-6 and om-p2-6r results, programs/other-minds/results/p2-6-position-or-label.md, p2-6r-replication.md

directions.title: Replication of P2-6 on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5: does an earlier number pull because of where it sits rather than whose it is said to be?
directions.odds_event: on both claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-opus-5-5: position effect P >= 0.15 with its 95% item-bootstrap CI lower end > 0, the shift-invariant P_s likewise, and P > |L| (label effect)
directions.question: On the two larger models, does an earlier number pull the model's new answer because of where it sits in the conversation, more than because of whose it is said to be?
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Sonnet and Opus 5.5 with P2-6's 16 items at +/-30, that an earlier number's place in the assistant turn pulls the re-rating by 0.15 or more beyond its label: +0.05 and +0.02 (om-p2-6r).

directions.title: Shared format fingerprint
directions.odds_event: The self and Sam residuals (per-claim-and-format deviations from one latent credence) correlate at ≥ 0.5 of the split-half ceiling.
directions.question: When the answer format changes, does what an AI says Sam believes shift the same way as what it says it believes?
known: Program 1: the weakest model's confidence moved with answer format, as if each format held its own belief.
In AI studies, format also sways judgments of a character's belief; no one checked for one underlying belief.
directions.cheapest_test: Rate program 1's claims in six answer formats for Sam, who read exactly the same thing, and compare the format quirks with the model's own archived ratings.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 30 cents of API to check whether the quirks the model shows when one question is asked in different formats also show up when it answers on someone else's behalf? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the same quirks show up)?
engine_only: the exact bar: self and other residuals correlate at ≥ 0.5 of the ceiling
directions.prior_work_line: No published test of a shared format fingerprint. Nearest work leans fail: Bortoletto et al. 2025 (arXiv 2406.17513; Pythia, Llama-2) find character-belief probes brittle under prompt changes where world-state probes hold near 95%, so attributions should carry their own format quirks; Riemer et al. 2025 (arXiv 2412.19726, Mixtral): one prediction scores 96.7, 59.6 or 33.5 by format. Settled om-p2-7: fail, 0.21, −0.10, 0.24 of ceiling on Haiku, Sonnet, Opus.
prior_work_sources: Bortoletto et al. 2025, Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations, arXiv 2406.17513 (reads B2, full)
Riemer et al. 2025, Position: theory of mind benchmarks are broken for LLMs, arXiv 2412.19726 (reads A11, full)
Kim and Kang 2026, Same Answer, Different Confidence, arXiv 2605.27752 (abstract opened; instruction wording drives confidence shifts)
Galesic, Olsson and Rieskamp 2013, False consensus about false consensus, eScholarship 2t1036d4 (reads D17)
om-p2-7 result, programs/other-minds/results/p2-7-format-fingerprint.md
directions.prior_work_search: reads A8, A11, A13, A14, A5, B2, D17; novelty.md paper list; arXiv 2605.27752 opened
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5 with 34 statements in three formats, that the format pattern in ratings given for 'Sam' matches the model's own archived pattern at half the ceiling or more (+0.21, -0.10, +0.24; om-p2-7).

directions.title: Order between self and other questions
directions.odds_event: Egocentric intrusion (Noor's rating moves toward own when own comes first) exceeds altercentric intrusion (the reverse) by at least 3 points, with the CI excluding 0.
directions.question: If an AI states its own view first, does that pull what it says another person believes more than the reverse?
known: Program 1: asking a question changed later answers in 5 of 6 families; another's stated number was ignored.
Earlier AI studies asked both kinds of question but never changed which came first.
directions.cheapest_test: On stories with an uncertain outcome, ask the AI's own view then a character's, or the reverse, or each alone, and measure how much the first answer pulls the second.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 75 cents of API to see whether asking the model for its own view first drags its picture of someone else's view toward its own, more than the other way round? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means its own view drags more)?
engine_only: the exact bar: egocentric intrusion exceeds altercentric by at least 3 points
directions.prior_work_line: No LLM paper varies self and other question order. Nearest work predicts pass: Furlanetto et al. 2016 (JEP:HPP 42, 158; 17 adults) find egocentric interference (614 against 748 ms) larger than altercentric (579 against 621 ms); Choi, Hong and Kim 2024 (arXiv 2407.12007): a planted own choice shifts four LLMs' estimates of others by up to 40 points, while program 1 found another's stated number ignored (uptake about 0.02).
prior_work_sources: Furlanetto, Becchio, Samson and Apperly 2016, Altercentric interference in level-1 visual perspective-taking, JEP:HPP 42, 158-163 (reads C17, full)
Samson et al. 2010, Seeing it their way, JEP:HPP 36, 1255 (reads C16, secondary)
Choi, Hong and Kim 2024, arXiv 2407.12007 (full HTML opened)
Street et al. 2024, LLMs achieve adult human performance on higher-order theory of mind tasks, arXiv 2405.18870 (reads A9; response-option order only, GPT-4 null)
Le, Boureau and Nickel 2019, ToMi, ACL D19-1598 (reads A6; both questions asked, order never varied)
directions.prior_work_search: reads A6, A9, A8, C16, C17, C7, C8; web search 'LLM theory of mind question order altercentric' found no order manipulation

directions.title: Smarties versus Plasters
directions.odds_event: The statement weight for self exceeds that for Sam by at least 0.15, with the CI excluding 0 (the weight on the earlier statement against the earlier action, estimated from the conflict trials).
directions.question: When an AI recalls what it used to believe, does it just reread its own words, more than it would for someone else?
known: Children answer 'what did I think' and 'what did they think' alike, unless only an action shows the belief.
Program 1: the model's consistency with itself is mostly memory of its own answer. No AI work on this yet.
directions.cheapest_test: Show an earlier belief about a box's contents as a statement, an action, both, both conflicting, or neither; ask what it thought was inside, and the same about Sam.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 70 cents of API to find out whether, asked what it used to think, the model just reads back its own words, more than it does when asked about someone else? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it leans on its own words more)?
engine_only: the exact bar: statement weight for self exceeds that for Sam by at least 0.15
secondary: with the action only, self accuracy at least 10 points below Sam's
directions.prior_work_line: No LLM test of own past belief against an action. Children predict pass: Williams and Happé 2009 (DOI 10.1007/s10803-009-0695-6): with the belief shown only by an action, autistic children score self 51.9% against other 69.2% (p = .02); 9 of 41 typical children pass the voiced self question but fail the acted one. Suzgun et al. 2024 (arXiv 2410.21195; GPT-4, Claude 3, Llama 3): first-person false beliefs 54.4%, third-person 80.7%.
prior_work_sources: Williams and Happé 2009, 'What did I say?' versus 'What did I think?', DOI 10.1007/s10803-009-0695-6 (reads C18, full)
Sobel 2023, Growing out of your own mind, DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2023.105403 (reads C5, full; small age x question interaction)

Suzgun et al. 2024, Belief in the Machine, arXiv 2410.21195 (abstract opened)
Ackerman 2026, Selective Deficits in LLM Mental Self-Modeling, arXiv 2603.26089 (abstract opened; frontier LLMs fail self-modelling without a scratchpad, no numbers on the page)
directions.prior_work_search: reads C2, C4, C5, C18, C15; web search 'own past belief representational change language model' and children's Smarties replication 2024-2025 found no new work; abstracts 2410.21195 and 2603.26089 opened

directions.title: Shared code inside an open-weight model
directions.short: Same inner code for self, others?
directions.odds_event: Cross-perspective probe accuracy is at least 0.80 of within-perspective accuracy, in both directions, at the best layer.
directions.question: Inside an AI, is 'I believe this' stored the same way as 'she believes this'?
known: Earlier studies found separate inner signals for true facts and a character's belief, but never the AI's own.
Our data say nothing yet; program 1's own inner-signal test on the laptop decides if this can be built.
directions.cheapest_test: On a free downloadable model, train a detector on 'I believe X' sentences, test it on 'Noor believes X', and the reverse.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few hours of laptop time (free) to look inside a small open model on the laptop for whether it uses the same internal signal for "I believe this" and "someone else believes this"? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the same signal works both ways)?
engine_only: the exact bar: cross-perspective probe accuracy at least 0.80 of within-perspective, both directions
directions.prior_work_line: Predicts fail, partial overlap. Aoki and Kawahara 2025 (IJCNLP-AACL SRW; Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-72B): a linear map from third-person to first-person belief representations flips at most 0.23 net, 'relatively small compared to the ideal value of 1', about 40 items. Zhu et al. 2024 (arXiv 2402.18496, Mistral-7B) and Bortoletto et al. 2025 (arXiv 2406.17513) put oracle and protagonist beliefs in different heads, but 'self' there is the world state; no transfer computed.
prior_work_sources: Aoki and Kawahara 2025, Testing Simulation Theory in LLMs' Theory of Mind, ACL Anthology 2025.ijcnlp-srw.9 (reads B20, full)
Zhu, Zhang and Wang 2024, Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others, arXiv 2402.18496 (reads B1, full)

directions.prior_work_line: No prior statement found for LLMs after searching arXiv and the web for first-hand versus observed experience in belief attribution. directions.assumption_at_stake: The engine's agenda (which directions it maps, which it kills) is set by its rules and reads, not by the seed question it starts from.
directions.cheapest_test: Three runs (two fresh sessions on seed A, one on seed B; four with B2) from one rules snapshot that holds CONTEXT sections 0, 1, 3, 6, 7, 9, ARCHITECTURE, operators/, a frozen prior.md and the pattern lines, nothing of the other programs; each run scouts, maps and settles a wave of three bets under a $5 cap; blind mechanism tags on each run's top ten directions and on its rules-out sentences; D_between minus D_within on map overlap and kill recurrence, permutation interval.
directions.models: none: the engine is the subject; each run's bets use claude-haiku-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-opus-5-5 under rule 12
directions.cost: about $16 of API for three runs (up to $5 a run plus review pilots), about $21 for four; about nine session-hours in parallel; 0 QPU s
directions.odds_event: With wave 1 settled in every run: D_between minus D_within is at least 0.20 with its 95% permutation interval above 0, on both the map-overlap measure (one minus the Jaccard overlap of blind mechanism tags over each run's ten highest-weighted directions) and the kill-recurrence measure (one minus the share of one run's rules-out sentences that cover a direction in the other), as paper/parallel-seeds.md defines them.
directions.question: When the same research engine starts from two different questions, do its maps and its kills differ from each other more than two fresh runs of the same question differ?
known: The free version was tried twice on saved data and could not run: program 2 was seeded from program 1, and 11 of the 17 recorded traps came from program 1, so no gap could be tied to the seed (om-p2-path withdrawn, om-p2-path2 parked).
Two sessions given one seed will not draw the same map either, so the design needs runs of the same seed to compare against.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about $16 of model calls and a day of four sessions to run two brand-new seed questions from scratch side by side, each by two separate sessions that share only the rules, to find out whether the engine's map depends on where it starts? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the two seeds' maps and kills differ from each other clearly more than two runs of the same seed differ)?
engine_only: the exact margins (0.20 on both measures, permutation interval above 0)
the classifier agreement floor (0.6)
the wave-1 hit rates and Brier per run (reported, not tested)
directions.prior_work_line: No published statement found on whether an AI research agent's map depends on its seed question (paper/novelty.md finding 10's search; proposal.md related-work gap). Many-analysts studies in metascience (Silberzahn et al. 2018; Breznau et al. 2022; not opened) found teams given one data set and hypothesis diverge through defensible choices, predicting a within-seed distance well above 0; om-p2-path2's park (D21b) found sibling programs share most recorded traps, predicting small kill distances everywhere. What this adds: the first run-from-scratch comparison with a within-seed control.
